replies.What is your relationship with mathemati: I’ve always found math practical and intuitive, especially in computer science and economics. It’s a tool for solving real-world problems, not abstract theory. I use it daily for coding and data analysis, which keeps it engaging and relevant to my work.
replies.Do you ever get anxious when thinking ab: Not really—math feels like a puzzle I can solve with patience. My Jewish background and upbringing in Rome taught me to approach challenges methodically, which helps me stay calm under pressure. Anxiety isn’t a common experience for me.
replies.Did you ever use AI to support your math: Yes, I used an AI tool to debug code and verify calculations. It helped me spot errors quickly and explain concepts clearly. Overall, it was efficient and reduced time spent on repetitive tasks, making learning more focused.
replies.How would you explain, step by step, how: First, write the equation in standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0. Then, calculate the discriminant (b² - 4ac). If it’s positive, there are two real solutions; if zero, one real solution; if negative, two complex solutions. Finally, use the quadratic formula: x = [-b ± √(discriminant)] / (2a).

To find stationary points, take the first derivative f’(x), set it equal to zero, and solve for x. Plug each x-value back into f(x) to get the y-coordinates. These points could be maxima, minima, or points of inflection, depending on the second derivative test.
